conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your transplant team doctors. I understand you came in today with nausea and vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. I woke up this morning feeling really nauseous and threw up a couple times. But it’s better now—I’m actually hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear the nausea is improving. You mentioned some pain over your graft site when you arrived—how’s that feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s not really painful now. Just a little fullness. But I haven’t had a bowel movement in three days, and I haven’t passed gas either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s important. We’ve ordered a KUB X-ray and a renal ultrasound to check things out. Constipation can definitely cause discomfort, especially after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying to stay regular. I’m on senna and Colace. But nothing’s moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help with that. The imaging will give us a clearer picture. We also need to check your kidney function and make sure your transplant is doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your KUB came back. It shows moderate fecal loading in the colon—so yes, you’re quite constipated. But no blockage, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s probably why I’ve been feeling so bloated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re going to start with milk of magnesia. If that doesn’t work, we may need an enema. We want to avoid straining or discomfort near your graft site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my kidney? Is it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound shows your transplanted kidneys are working well—your urine output is good and your creatinine is around 1.4, which is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But the report mentioned something about fluid around the kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s a large fluid collection around the transplant site. It’s been there since your last admission. We’re watching it closely, but it hasn’t changed much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous? Could it get infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring for that. You’re already on micafungin through your PICC line to prevent infection, especially since you had Candida before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I remember. And my WBC is low again, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your white count is between 2.3 and 3.0. It’s low, likely due to your anti-rejection meds. We’ve reduced your Valcyte dose to help protect your bone marrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that increase my risk of infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re balancing risks. Lowering Valcyte helps your counts, but we’re keeping you on other protections like micafungin and monitoring closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How did you sleep? Any bowel movement yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not yet. I took the milk of magnesia, but nothing happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try a soap suds enema today. If that doesn’t work, we’ll add lactulose. We really want to get things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The enema helped a little, but not fully. We’re starting lactulose—30 mL daily. That should help soften things up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. My belly feels so tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re also watching your blood pressure. It’s been a bit low, so we’ve reduced your amlodipine and carvedilol doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a little dizzy when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from the lower BP. We’ll keep an eye on it. Also, your Prograf level was high yesterday—16.6.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High? I thought higher was better for preventing rejection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Too high can be toxic—cause kidney issues or tremors. We lowered your dose to 3 mg twice daily. Today’s level is 11.2, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So we’re aiming for a sweet spot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We want enough to prevent rejection, but not so much that it harms you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your labs show your creatinine is stable at 1.2, and you passed three stools after the lactulose. Your constipation is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If things keep going this well, probably tomorrow. We’ll remove the wound VAC today—the site is small and clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a regular dressing after that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, saline damp-to-dry dressing once a day. You can shower, but no baths or swimming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge today. Your condition is stable—clear mind, walking on your own, eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? Anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Prograf is now 3 mg twice daily, carvedilol is 12.5 mg twice daily, and Valcyte is 450 mg daily. You’ll also take lactulose as needed for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the micafungin through the PICC?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that daily until the end date on the prescription. Home health will help with that and your dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the clinic if you have fever, nausea, vomiting, constipation, redness at the incision, or decreased urine output. Check your weight daily—let us know if you gain 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Twice weekly. Don’t take your Prograf until after your blood is drawn. Bring the dose with you so you can take it right after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.
